quote: But then the clever arguer can make you believe anything they choose, if there is a sufficient variety of signs to selectively report. That doesn’t sound right.
content: Kamenica and Gentzkow's receiver is never deceived. Bayes-plausibility means every posterior the sender induces is calibrated for the information actually received, and the average posterior equals the prior. The sender gains by shaping the receiver's actions through how information is partitioned, not by getting the receiver to believe falsehoods. That is the essay's resolution in theorem form: a receiver who conditions on the sender's algorithm cannot be made to "believe anything they choose," which is the claim the essay flagged with "That doesn't sound right" and then dissolved (Kamenica & Gentzkow 2011). The essay's intuition does not sit between two theorems. It is the belief-side content of the first one.

quote: Between the prosecution and the defense, someone has a motive to present any given piece of evidence, so the court will see all the evidence; that is the theory.
content: "Most legal processes" should have been "Anglo-American legal processes," and civil-law systems do use an investigating magistrate. The essay's verdict on the adversarial theory is closer to Fable's than Fable allows. The next sentence says: "Reality often has many-sided problems, and deep problems, and nonobvious answers, which are not readily found by Blues and Greens screaming at each other." The laboratory evidence also supports the essay's "almost as good" for the two-box case. Thibaut and Walker's group found that adversarial advocates searched harder for evidence when the initial facts were against their client, offsetting the bias of the first evidence found. Two advocates on a binary question do reasonably well, and many-sided questions defeat the system. That is what the essay says.

quote: In a way, no one can really trust the theory of natural selection until after they have listened to creationists for five minutes; and then they know it’s solid.
content: The sentence comes after the essay's paragraph about the familiar case: "If you're ticked off by a contrary argument, then you are familiar with the case." It concerns a listener who can evaluate what the creationist says. For that listener, filtered-evidence logic applies: if five minutes of the other side's best material is weak, that is evidence the theory is solid. Koehler's effect concerns something else, how one dissenting expert changes a layperson's estimate of expert consensus (Koehler 2016). That is a judgment about authority, not about arguments. Inoculation, which Fable grants works, is the case where the listener already has the refutations, and in this book the listener has them.
